HOOK
Divers pulled a rusty lump off the sea floor... and inside it was a computer. Two thousand years old.

Underwater, sunbeams and bubbles; two cartoon divers in brass helmets haul a green-crusted lump out of the sand; it glints and a gear tooth peeks out. Smash to a title-less cut to a calendar of a ticking hand.
Low macro on the lump, then a fast pull-back up through the water to the boat above
Hushed, curious; slow on 'computer', a beat, then 'Two thousand years old.'
SETUP
In 1901, Greek sponge divers lifted treasure from an ancient shipwreck. Most of it was easy to understand. One piece looked like junk.
Sunny Greek harbour, white houses, blue water; crates of treasure on the dock; a shrugging museum clerk holds up the green lump between two shiny golden objects.
Wide crane down from the sky to the dock, push in on the clerk
Matter of fact, then a dry 'One piece looked like junk.'
PLAN
So it sat in a museum, and for a long time nobody knew what it was.
Dusty museum storeroom; the lump on a shelf under a cobweb, a cat sleeps on it, visitors walk past without looking; the clock on the wall spins through the years.
Slow side track along the shelf, time-lapse light moving across the wall
Gentle, a little funny.
BUT
But when scientists finally looked inside with X-rays, they found gears.
A scientist in a long coat slides the lump into a huge humming scanner; the screen flickers; a pair of eyes go wide; gear shapes glow on the monitor.
Dutch tilt close-up on the scientist's eyes, then push into the glowing screen
'But' flat, then rising on 'gears'.
THEN
More than thirty tiny bronze gears, all fitted together like the inside of a watch.
Exploded view: the gears float apart in the air, spinning, tiny teeth labelled by painted arrows; they click back into a golden box.
Orbiting camera around the floating gears, ending on a close-up of two meshing teeth
Wondering, building.
CONFLICT
And that should have been impossible. Nothing this complicated was known for another thousand years.
A timeline painted on a long scroll rolls across the screen: 'THIS' stands alone at the left, then a huge empty gap, then medieval clocks at the right; a scientist scratches his head in the gap.
Fast side track along the scroll through the empty gap, whip-pan to the scratching scientist
Serious, 'impossible' slow and flat.
PIVOT
You see,
Pause-frame: a single gear turning in the dark, spotlight on it.
Slow push-in on one tooth
Lean in. A beat of silence before and after.
PIVOT2
scans found hidden writing that explained how it worked. Turn the crank, and the gears moved pointers across the sky.
Tiny engraved letters glow on the plate; a Greek scholar in a toga turns a small crank; dials show a sun and a moon sliding along a ring of stars.
Extreme close-up on glowing letters, then pull back to the scholar turning the crank
Clear, explaining a secret.
ESCALATION
One dial showed the phases of the moon. Another warned of eclipses. A third counted the years between the Olympic games.
Three dials in turn: a moon that waxes and wanes, a sun sliding into shadow, a runner with a torch crossing a tiny stadium.
Smooth side track from dial to dial, rack focus between them
Building, each one a step brighter.
SO
So around two thousand years ago, someone built a machine the size of a shoebox that could predict the sky.
A shoebox-sized brass machine on a workbench in a candle-lit Greek workshop; an old craftsman files a tooth by hand, then proudly pushes the crank and the sky inside glows.
High crane down into the workshop, slow push to the craftsman's smile
Warm, impressed.
PAYOFF
Nobody knows who made it. Nothing like it appeared again for over a thousand years.
Silhouette of the craftsman; the machine is wrapped in cloth and loaded onto a ship; the ship sails into a stormy sunset; the timeline gap stretches.
Wide sweeping pull-back over the sea as the ship becomes tiny
Quiet, a little sad.
CLOSE
The ancient Greeks built a computer, and the sea kept it for two thousand years.
The ship sinks; the green lump settles on the sandy sea floor among fish; sunbeams fade to deep blue; one gear catches the light.
Slow dive down through the water to the lump, hold on one glinting gear
Slow, soft, final. Hard stop, then the ta-ding.
